question: Mr. Lopez has a choice of two routes to get to work. Route A is \(6\) miles long, and his average speed along this route is \(30\) miles per hour. Route B is \(5\) miles long, and his average speed along this route is \(40\) miles per hour, except for a \(\tfrac{1}{2}\)-mile stretch in a school zone where his average speed is \(20\) miles per hour. By how many minutes is Route B quicker than Route A?
solution:
Route B has two different speeds, so its travel time is the sum of the times on the two stretches. Use \(\text{time}=\text{distance}/\text{speed}\).

Route A takes
\[
t_A=\frac{6}{30}=\frac15\text{ hour}.
\]
On Route B, the distance outside the school zone is \(5-\tfrac12=\tfrac92\) miles. Therefore
\[
t_B=\frac{9/2}{40}+\frac{1/2}{20}
=\frac9{80}+\frac1{40}
=\frac{11}{80}\text{ hour}.
\]
The time saved is
\[
t_A-t_B=\frac{16}{80}-\frac{11}{80}
=\frac5{80}=\frac1{16}\text{ hour}.
\]
Multiplying by \(60\) converts this to minutes:
\[
\frac1{16}\cdot60=\frac{15}{4}=\boxed{3\tfrac34}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\text{(B)}\).
